patterns.usage_note: こた is the spoken contraction of ことは, so it turns up wherever topicalized こと would: most often in the concessive frame 〜こた〜が ('do it I did, but …') and in 〜こたない ('there's no need to'). It is casual and a little rough, at home in male-sounding speech and in fiction dialogue, and out of place in anything written or polite. Spell out the full ことは in any register above plain conversation.

examples.ruby: 連絡[れんらく]するこたするが、期待[きたい]はしないでくれ。
examples.english: I'll get in touch, sure, but don't get your hopes up.

examples.ruby: 読[よ]んだこた読[よ]んだが、内容[ないよう]は覚[おぼ]えていない。
examples.english: Read it I did, but I don't remember a thing about it.

examples.ruby: 安[やす]いこた安[やす]いけど、すぐ壊[こわ]れそうだ。
examples.english: Cheap it certainly is, but it looks like it'll break right away.

patterns.usage_note: The all-purpose nominalizer, used for concrete events the speaker directly perceives or experiences, which is why verbs of perception take only の as the complement marker (転ぶのを見た, never 転ぶことを見た). こと is the abstract counterpart, and it is the required one when the nominalization is itself the predicate (私の趣味は絵を描くことだ, not …描くのだ, which means something else entirely) and in fixed frames such as ことがある or ことにする. With likes, dislikes, difficulty and speed (好きだ, 難しい, 速い) either is possible, and の is the more conversational choice.

examples.ruby: 朝[あさ]早[はや]く起[お]きるのは本当[ほんとう]につらい。
examples.english: Getting up early in the morning is genuinely rough.

examples.ruby: 彼[かれ]が嘘[うそ]をついたのはすぐに分[わ]かった。
examples.english: It was obvious right away that he'd lied.

examples.ruby: 弟[おとうと]が階段[かいだん]で転[ころ]ぶのを見[み]てしまった。
examples.english: I happened to see my little brother take a tumble on the stairs.
